\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can end a Kannada conversation politely and choose a farewell that fits the situation.}

Part three ways without ever saying a blunt goodbye, and say what hōgi baruttēne promises instead.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hōgu]{\kn{ಹೋಗು} (hōgu) — \textquotedblleft{}go,\textquotedblright{} and \kn{ಬಾ} (come)}

\label{lesson:KA-C04-hoogu}



\begin{quote}
Two everyday verbs — and together they make the Kannada goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೋ}} (\emph{hō}, \emph{ha} + long-\emph{ō} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ಗು}} (\emph{gu}) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗು}} (\emph{hōgu}). Its partner: \textbf{\kn{ಬಾ}} (\emph{bā}, \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗು}} (\emph{hōgu}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\kn{ಬಾ}} (\emph{bā}, \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) are native Dravidian verbs. As commands they are whole words: \emph{hōgu!} (\textquotedblleft{}go!\textquotedblright{}), \emph{bā!} (\textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{}). You need both, because Kannada — like every Dravidian language — does not say a plain \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{} It says \textquotedblleft{}I go, and I \textbf{come back}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}hōgu\textquotedblright{} (go) and \textquotedblleft{}bā\textquotedblright{} (come)
  \item \emph{Say it:} why you need both to say goodbye (Kannada's farewell is \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hēge}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{hōgu} and \emph{bā} mean, and why will you need both to part? (\textquotedblleft{}Go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}; the Kannada goodbye is \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\kn{◌ಿ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S04-vowel-sign-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌್} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ಿ}} — \emph{i}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{i}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{◌ಿ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} \emph{sari} — okay / alright / correct (sari)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā} — how are you? (respectful)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ}} \emph{cennāgi} — well, nicely — and the reply \textquotedblleft{}\kn{ನಾನು} \kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ}} \emph{paravāgilla} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ಿ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ಿ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌ಿ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಸರಿ}  ·  \kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌ಿ} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{◌ಿ} once more
\end{itemize}

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hōgi baruttēne]{\kn{ಹೋಗಿ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ} (hōgi baruttēne) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C04-hoogi-baruttene}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Kannada goodbye — a promise, not a parting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗಿ}} (\emph{hōgi}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) is \emph{hōgu} + the \textquotedblleft{}-i\textquotedblright{} that means \textquotedblleft{}having …d.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\kn{ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ}} (\emph{baruttēne}, \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) is from \emph{baru} (\textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) + present + \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗಿ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ}} = \textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗಿ}} (\emph{hōgi}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ}} (\emph{baruttēne}, \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having gone, I come {[}back{]}},\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{} A Kannada speaker never signs off with a bare \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{} — it sounds final. It is the same \textquotedblleft{}go-and-come-back\textquotedblright{} farewell across the Dravidian south (Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}, Telugu \emph{veḷḷi vastānu}, Malayalam \emph{pōyi varāṁ}). The warm reply is \textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗಿ} \kn{ಬನ್ನಿ}} (\emph{hōgi banni}, \textquotedblleft{}go and come {[}back{]}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}having …d\textquotedblright{} participle}]
\emph{Hōgi} chains actions: \textquotedblleft{}having gone, (then) I come.\textquotedblright{} Kannada, like its sisters, strings verbs with one in the participle form and the last one fully conjugated.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family — the same idea, five ways}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{} (goodbye)} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Kannada} & \emph{hōgi baruttēne} \\
Tamil & \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} \\
Telugu & \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} \\
Malayalam & \emph{pōyi varāṃ} \\
Bengali (Indo-Aryan) & \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The whole south, and beyond, prefers a promise of return to a blunt farewell.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the goodbye — \emph{hōgi baruttēne}
  \item its literal meaning (\textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}I'll come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{hōgi banni}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Kannada goodbye literally promise, and how do you answer? (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}; reply \emph{hōgi banni}, \textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāḷe sigōṇa]{\kn{ನಾಳೆ} \kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ} (nāḷe sigōṇa) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C04-naale-sigona}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye with a date on it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾಳೆ}} (\emph{nāḷe}): \textbf{\kn{ನಾ}} (\emph{nā}) + \textbf{\kn{ಳೆ}} (\emph{ḷe}, with the retroflex \textbf{\kn{ಳ}} \emph{ḷ}). \textbf{\kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} (\emph{sigōṇa}) = \emph{sigu} (\textquotedblleft{}meet, be found\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-ōṇa} (\textquotedblleft{}let's\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾಳೆ}} (\emph{nāḷe}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, from \textbf{\kn{ನಾಳ್}} (\emph{nāḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}) — the very same \emph{nāḷ} behind Tamil's \emph{nāḷai}. \textbf{\kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} (\emph{sigōṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{}) is from \textbf{\kn{ಸಿಗು}} (\emph{sigu}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet, to be found\textquotedblright{}) — so the phrase is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow, let's meet}.\textquotedblright{} The \textbf{-\kn{ಓಣ}} (\emph{-ōṇa}) ending is Kannada's warm \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{}: \emph{hōgōṇa} (\textquotedblleft{}let's go\textquotedblright{}), \emph{tinnōṇa} (\textquotedblleft{}let's eat\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāḷe sigōṇa\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nāḷ}, shared with Tamil \emph{nāḷai})
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} ending (\emph{-ōṇa})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{nāḷe sigōṇa}, and what Tamil word shares the \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} root? (\emph{Nāḷe} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{sigu} \textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}; Tamil \emph{nāḷai} — both from \emph{nāḷ} \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[matte sigōṇa]{\kn{ಮತ್ತೆ} \kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ} (matte sigōṇa) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C04-matte-sigona}



\begin{quote}
The open-ended, warm goodbye — no date, just a promise.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ಮತ್ತೆ}} (\emph{matte}): note the doubled \textbf{\kn{ತ್ತ}} (\emph{tt}). \textbf{\kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} (\emph{sigōṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{}) you just learned.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಮತ್ತೆ} \kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} = \textbf{\kn{ಮತ್ತೆ}} (\emph{matte}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} (\emph{sigōṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}.\textquotedblright{} Both words are native Dravidian: \emph{matte} (\textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{sigu} (\textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}). Where Tamil's \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mīṇḍum sandippōm}) reaches for the Sanskrit loan \emph{sandi} to say \textquotedblleft{}meet,\textquotedblright{} Kannada keeps the native \emph{sigu} — the same phrase, from home-grown stock.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}matte sigōṇa\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{matte}, \emph{sigōṇa})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the phrase mean, and which native verb does Kannada use for \textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet again\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sigu} — where Tamil borrowed the Sanskrit \emph{sandi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:KA-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The farewells}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the everyday goodbye — \emph{hōgi baruttēne} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{hōgi banni} (\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāḷe sigōṇa}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{matte sigōṇa}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two verbs (\emph{hōgu} go, \emph{bā} come)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nāḷ}), \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{matte}, \emph{sigōṇa})
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} ending (\emph{-ōṇa})
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hōgi baruttēne} — \textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{}; the Dravidian promise-of-return goodbye
  \item \emph{nāḷe} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nāḷ} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} (shared with Tamil \emph{nāḷai}); \emph{sigu} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} (native)
  \item \emph{matte} \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} — where Tamil borrowed Sanskrit \emph{sandi} for \textquotedblleft{}meet,\textquotedblright{} Kannada kept \emph{sigu}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Kannada never say a plain \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving,\textquotedblright{} and what does its everyday goodbye promise instead? (It sounds too final; \emph{hōgi baruttēne} promises \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
